idiom_name: typed hook + getters whose return types compose with the element props
implementation_notes: TypeScript changes nothing mechanically - a hook owns the state and returns getters - but the types become the contract the consumer codes against: a getter's return type must compose with the element's own props (React.ComponentProps<'button'> plus the primitive's extras), the state can be a discriminated union so impossible states do not render, and generics let one primitive serve any item type. The mainstream headless libraries ship typed APIs for exactly this reason: Radix Primitives documents 'a fully-typed API' plus an asChild prop 'giving users full control over the rendered element'. In a TypeScript project the getter signatures are the documentation.
pitfalls: Getter return types that do not merge with the element's props force consumers into as-casts, which is where mis-spread props hide.
Generics on getters erase the item type unless the call passes the payload; inference from index alone gives you a list of unknowns.
Ref forwarding/merging has two different React types (Ref<T> vs RefObject<T>); a getter that types its ref loosely breaks consumers who need the DOM node.
A state object spread as any loses the discriminated-union protection the state type was added for.

variants.name: Vue: composable plus scoped slots
variants.idiom_name: useX() composable publishes state; scoped slots hand markup back to the call site
variants.implementation_notes: Vue's documentation defines a composable as 'a function that leverages Vue's Composition API to encapsulate and reuse stateful logic', and describes the renderless component - a component that encapsulates logic and delegates all visual output to the consumer through scoped slots - while noting that most of what renderless components achieve is done more efficiently with the Composition API because it avoids the extra component nesting. The practical realization is therefore a composable for the state plus a scoped slot (or plain component with named slots) where the markup must stay in the template: the slot props carry the state, the composable carries the behaviour.
variants.code_sketch:
<!-- behaviour: composable plus (optionally) a component with a scoped slot -->
<script setup>
const { isOpen, toggle, panelProps } = useDisclosure()
</script>
<template>
  <button :aria-expanded="isOpen" @click="toggle">Details</button>
  <section v-if="isOpen" v-bind="panelProps"><slot :open="isOpen" /></section>
</template>
pitfalls: Destructuring a reactive object returned by a composable loses reactivity unless toRefs() is used, and the type system will not warn you.
Lifecycle helpers (onMounted/onUnmounted) only register when called synchronously during setup; calling them from an async callback silently loses the registration.
Slot content is compiled in the parent's scope, so a child's state must travel through slot props; reaching for the child's internals breaks the contract.

variants.name: Angular: headless directives over consumer HTML
variants.idiom_name: headless directives (Angular Aria) over consumer-supplied HTML structure
variants.implementation_notes: Angular's ecosystem ships the pattern as directives rather than components: Angular Aria is documented as 'a collection of headless, accessible directives that implement common WAI-ARIA patterns' whose directives handle keyboard interactions, ARIA attributes, focus management and screen-reader support, while 'all you have to do is provide the HTML structure, CSS styling, and business logic'. Where no such directive exists, content projection (<ng-content>) plus a behavioural directive reproduces the split: the component template marks projection points and the consumer's markup is projected in, so the consumer owns the DOM while the directive owns behaviour.
variants.code_sketch: {{ o.label }}
pitfalls: A directive can only attach to an element that exists: conditional rendering (@if) around the host element silently drops the behaviour for that branch.
<ng-content> is resolved at compile time and cannot be inserted or removed at run time, and hidden projections still instantiate their content.
Directives compose through DI tokens on the host element; a missing provider throws only when the directive actually reads it, so wiring errors surface late.
